lessons.title: Use the official starting-a-business map
lessons.html:
This course is a map. It shows official pages you can use if you want to start a small activity or micro-business in Canada, especially in Alberta. It does not say you will earn money. It is not legal, tax, or licensing advice. It does not replace a lawyer, an accountant, or a registry agent.

The Government of Canada's Starting a business page lists steps to consider before you operate a business:

  1. Planning a business
  2. Choosing a business name
  3. Registering your business with the government
  4. Applying for business permits and licences
  5. Getting business support and financing
  6. Free tax help for your business

You may not need every step on the first day. Selling a few items at a local market is not the same as hiring staff. The map helps you see which official page to open next.

This course walks through three parts of that map: how businesses are set up (the structure), when you may need a CRA business number, and where Alberta registries and licences live. For permits, you will also see BizPaL, a Government of Canada tool that lists permits and licences.

Start from the official pages, not from a social media ad or a paid “we will register you” site. Rules change. Check the live government page before you pay a fee or sign a form.

If you already keep invoices or GST records, that is a different skill. This course does not teach bookkeeping or tax filing.

lessons.title: Name the common business structures
lessons.html:
Before you register anything, it helps to know the common business structures in Canada. The CRA says the structure you choose has a significant effect on the way you report your income, and on many other matters. This lesson names the structures. It does not tell you which one to pick.

A sole proprietorship is an unincorporated business owned by one person. The CRA calls it the simplest kind of business structure. The owner makes the decisions, receives the profits, claims the losses, and does not have separate legal status from the business. The owner also assumes the risks of the business. Those risks can reach personal property and assets. You may register a business name, operate under your own name, or both.

A partnership, on the CRA page, is an association or relationship between two or more individuals, corporations, trusts, or partnerships that join together to carry on a trade or business. Partners contribute money, labour, property, or skills. In return, each partner is entitled to a share of the profits or losses. The Government of Alberta says partners share the profits and the risks or debts of the business.

A corporation is a separate legal entity. It can enter into contracts and own property in its own name. Alberta’s incorporation page says a corporation acts as a “person.” It can buy, sell, and own assets, including land, make contracts, sue, and be sued. You do not need to be a large business to register as a corporation. A small business with only one owner can do so.

Alberta’s registry pages say that if you need help deciding whether a sole proprietorship, partnership, or corporation is the best form, you should get legal advice. That is the right next step. This course will not choose for you.

lessons.title: When you may need a business number
lessons.html:
A business number (BN) is the standard identifier the CRA uses for a business or legal entity. Alberta’s Common Business Number page describes it as a federal 9-digit number.

Not every business must get a BN. The CRA says you need a BN if you need a GST/HST, payroll, or another CRA program account, or if you incorporate your business. If your business is unincorporated, you only need a BN when you register for program accounts with the CRA.

You can have only one BN for the same business or legal entity. New CRA program accounts are added to the BN you already have.

Registering with the CRA is not the only way to get a BN. The CRA says you may also receive one if you incorporate federally, or if you register or incorporate in certain provinces. Alberta is on that CRA list. Alberta partners with the CRA. After you form a corporation or non-profit organization, or register a business name, a federal business number is assigned. Alberta says there is no cost to obtain a business number.

When your information is entered at Corporate Registry, you receive proof of filing. Alberta says you will get an email when the federal business number is issued, unless one has already been assigned to you.

This course does not say whether you must register for GST/HST or payroll. Those are tax questions. Open the CRA’s “When you need a BN” page, and get help from the CRA or a qualified advisor if you are unsure.

lessons.title: Find Alberta registries and register the right thing
lessons.html:
In Alberta, registering a business name and incorporating a corporation are different steps. Both are done through authorized service providers.

A business name, Alberta says, does not have a legal existence of its own. It is a name used to represent the business to the public. The sole proprietor or partners remain personally responsible for the debts and obligations of the business. Registering a name does not give you ownership of that name. It is proof that a particular business is using it.

A trade name (also called a sole proprietorship on that page) is used when an individual does business under a name other than their personal name. To register, you choose a name, may get an optional Business Name Report, complete a Declaration of Trade Name, and take your information to an authorized Corporate Registry service provider with valid ID and fee payment. You cannot put words such as “Limited,” “Incorporated,” or “Corporation” — or Ltd., Inc., or Corp. — at the end of a business name, because that would suggest you are running a corporation.

To incorporate an Alberta corporation you follow the longer checklist on Alberta’s incorporation page. That checklist includes a name with a legal element (such as Ltd. or Inc.), a NUANS report for most word names, required notices, at least one adult director, and an agent for service in Alberta. If your information meets the requirements, the service provider gives you a certificate of incorporation.

Find providers on Alberta’s “Find a business registry” page. Registry agents charge a service fee that is not regulated and may vary. There is also a government fee for certain registrations. This course does not quote those fees.

As of 10 November 2026 (America/Regina), Corporate Registry listed 780-427-7013, and 310-0000 before the number in Alberta.

lessons.title: Check licences and permits before you operate
lessons.html:
A business licence is not the same as a registered business name or a business number. You may need none, one, or several licences, depending on what you do and where you do it.

Alberta’s Consumer Programs page says it licenses some businesses and individuals, and registers charitable organizations, under laws such as the Consumer Protection Act. It is an offence to operate without the required licence or charitable registration. Other businesses may be licensed through other government departments, municipalities, or delegated agencies. Some businesses do not need any type of licence.

If you are not sure, contact the business licensing office. As of 10 November 2026 (America/Regina), Alberta listed 780-422-1335, toll free 310-0000 before the number in Alberta, and sartr.businesslicensing@gov.ab.ca.

A licence is not an endorsement by the Government of Alberta, and it does not guarantee the quality of goods or services.

You may also need permits and licences from federal, provincial or territorial, and municipal governments. Canada.ca points to BizPaL. Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada says BizPaL builds a personalized list of the documents you may need from those levels of government. Start from the official BizPaL page and follow the link to bizpal.ca.

This course cannot tell you which licence your activity needs. Use the official pages, ask the licensing office, and check your municipality. Do not treat a completed course as permission to operate.
